analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal aid to colleges whose students cannot repay loans, and rewards schools that help low-income students graduate.
analysis.headline: Introduced in October 2022 with support from a Democrat and a Republican, the bill was referred to the Senate education committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make colleges responsible for what happens to their students' loans. A college whose former students cannot manage even a $1 reduction on their loan principal within two years of leaving school would lose access to all federal student aid and Pell Grants. Colleges whose students carry large amounts of unpaid loan debt would pay a fee, and that money would fund grants to colleges with strong records of getting low- and moderate-income students through school, plus need-based aid and support services. It also directs the Education Department to publish repayment rates and report on what colleges can do to improve them.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and taxpayers gain twice: weak colleges whose graduates cannot pay down loans would lose federal money, and the fees collected from colleges with high unpaid-loan balances would pay for need-based aid and student support at schools that help low- and moderate-income students succeed. Borrowers choosing a college would also see published repayment rates for each school.

how_it_helps.text: A college where 15 percent or fewer of its borrowers reduce their loan principal by at least one dollar within two years of entering repayment would be cut off from all federal student aid programs for two additional fiscal years, with published rates and an appeal process.

Colleges whose students leave with large unpaid loan balances would make risk-sharing payments equal to 2 percent of that balance, capped at 2.5 percent of the college's non-auxiliary revenue, and the calculation adjusts for national unemployment so schools are not punished for a bad economy.

Those payments fund grants to colleges with repayment rates above 25 percent and strong records serving low- and moderate-income students, usable for need-based aid, academic and student support services, and accelerated learning programs.

Borrowers in graduate school, military service, Peace Corps, disability rehabilitation, or approved deferments would not count against their college's rate, and a government report would highlight practices that help colleges serving many low-income students improve repayment.

analysis.who_pays: Low-performing colleges pay directly: the worst lose all federal aid eligibility, and colleges with high unpaid-loan balances pay a fee. Some colleges could pass those costs on to students through higher tuition, and students at a disqualified college would lose access to federal loans and Pell Grants while it is shut out.

drawbacks.text: Repayment-based ratings can punish colleges that enroll many low-income students, whose graduates typically earn less and rely more on deferments, even when the education itself is sound; the bill's long list of deferment exemptions and its unemployment adjustment are an acknowledgment of exactly this problem, but the 15 percent cutoff with a three-year funding ban is a blunt instrument.

A college cut off from federal aid would take its students' access to loans and Pell Grants with it, so the sanction lands partly on current and future students rather than only on the institution's leadership or owners.
Colleges facing risk-sharing payments could raise tuition to cover the fee, converting an accountability cost into a student cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core bargain is sound in principle: colleges profit from federal loan dollars, so colleges should bear some cost when their graduates cannot pay those loans down, and redirecting the fees toward aid for low-income students is a real benefit. The main risk is fairness of the metric — a hard cutoff plus a funding ban could hit schools serving disadvantaged students harder than predatory ones, and displaced students would feel the sanction themselves. A better-designed version would phase penalties in rather than impose a cliff.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in October 2022, read twice, and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no action before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen introduced the bill on October 11, 2022, with Sen. Todd Young as a cosponsor; Sen. Angus King introduced it on Shaheen's behalf.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever recorded: the committee never held a hearing or markup, and the full Senate never considered it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges with poor student-loan repayment outcomes came out ahead: they faced no new accountability, no risk-sharing fees, and kept full access to federal student aid and loan dollars, while taxpayers continued absorbing loans that never get repaid.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Weak-performing colleges kept federal aid unchanged

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, which was introduced on her behalf by Sen. King.

against.name: Sen. Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat from New Hampshire sponsored the bill and a Republican from Indiana cosponsored it, and no vote on it was ever taken in either direction.

industries.note: These schools collect federal loan dollars while large shares of their former students cannot pay down a dollar of principal; the bill would cut off their federal aid and charge fees on unpaid balances. Their interest in keeping that money flowing runs directly against the students carrying the debt.

industries.industry: Colleges serving low- and moderate-income students
industries.note: The same bill offers them a grant program for need-based aid and student support, funded by fees on other colleges, but a low repayment rate could disqualify them entirely. The bill tries to soften this with deferment exemptions, an unemployment adjustment, and a report aimed at helping these schools improve.

industries.industry: Federal student loan system and taxpayers
industries.note: Taxpayers guarantee loans that may never be repaid; making colleges share the cost of unpaid balances and publishing each school's repayment rate shifts that risk back toward the institutions that benefit from enrollment.
